title: Introducing Kwi, a new KDE terminal emulator

comments.comment:
Possibly off-topic, but a fun fact from a native Korean speaker:

This is also how it came to bear its name: kwisin, or more typically gwisin, is a romanized form of 귀신—Korean for ghost. It's pronounced a little bit like kwee-shin.

The word is Sino-Korean, written 鬼神 in Chinese characters. The hanja corresponding to Kwi, the name of this terminal emulator, is 鬼, which on its own means ghost, spirit, or devil. Both 鬼神 and 鬼 mean nearly the same thing in Chinese and Japanese as well as Korean.

comments.comment:
There are quite a few tools supporting sixel. Like GNUPLOT.

I somewhat used sixel, but interaction with terminal multiplexers is obviously imperfect (and I want my detachable sessions), so I needed to run just one specific thing in a raw terminal. So now I moved the regular workflow to driving sxiv which is side by side to the terminal. But if I decide that having an exceptional session is worth the hassle, I guess I will still use sixel as the more classical standard sufficient for what I am likely to want.

It looks like now WezTerm has Unicode coverage incomparable with Konsole (stronger in one area and weaker in another), and sixel, and slightly incomparable but similar featureset otherwise. So if I migrate off Konsole I can keep sixel option open and go to something that does the unique part of the work in a fully memory-safe way (although of course rendering is horrible and needs libraries, so it's not much safety gained).

Apparently Contour terminal has sixel and better Unicode feature coverage. But not sure how much I trust all of their crash reports to be from assertions…

comments.comment: I have been honestly shocked in the past to learn that my terminal (not sure if it was Konsole or GNOME Terminal, it was a long time ago) was actually causing enough back pressure on stdout to slow down the very verbose debug output from some code I was working on. I triple checked before believing it wasn’t just printf and traced it to write(1,…) blocking. The terminal was pegging a CPU and my program was failing to peg one unless I redirected stdout to /dev/null

comments.comment:
Personally I would say that it’s just something you have to experience, similar to high refresh rate monitors. Obviously a slow terminal and a 60Hz display are fine, but for me personally, once you experience the smoother version, it recontextualises the ordinary version. It’s not a big enough difference that I would give up important features for it, but since I have very few features I require of a terminal, I’ve been happy using the minimal Foot terminal, which is very fast.

It is very much not about the throughput of how much work you’re getting done. It’s about the tactile feeling of a responsive terminal. And it’s just ever so slightly less likely to feel annoying and frustrating. It just makes me happy.

(Although, if you haven’t tried it, I recommend trying some high refresh rate monitors. Or, perhaps, don’t, if you want to avoid the chance of getting hooked as I did)

If I read Wikipedia in a terminal (which I sometimes do) and stumble into a long interwiki section, Konsole can stumble for around ~1s, Contour terminal is only a bit faster even though it talks about «actually fast», WezTerm draws rectangles and background-loads the fonts when there are too many, and Ghostty seems to just manage or maybe preload a good fallback.

And yeah, with software rendering GPU-reliant terminals are laggy.

I have looked at the repo, in Main.qml and SettingsPage.qml but haven't found any "show menu bar" option, which other KDE apps have. To be fair, Kwi is brand new and not released yet, so it's fine! :)

comments.comment:
To achieve things, Kwi builds on libghostty-vt from the excellent Ghostty project

Ugh. I was excited until I learned that it'd just be using a vibe coded terminal library.
comments.comment_plain:
> To achieve things, Kwi builds on libghostty-vt from the excellent Ghostty project

Ugh. I was excited until I learned that it'd just be using a vibe coded terminal library.

comments.comment:
You're obviously entitled to your own opinions on where your bar is for "vibe coded," but I started the project years before "vibe coding" was a thing, and I've carefully cared for and hand-coded the entire architecture that libghostty-vt is built on over years of dedicated, volunteer work. And along the way being helped by other real humans dedicated their own real time.

It's hugely insulting to me and others who have worked hard to produce a high quality library with trivialized dismissals of years of a humans actual craft and labor. A couple of our core maintainers are literally teenagers who can't afford and do not use any AI assistance, and our non-profit helps fund their work to produce high quality work, and has helped some acquire their first jobs ever. (Note: the non-profit also funds non-teenagers, haha, and at least one also uses zero AI assistance whatsoever and maintains a large swath of Ghostty)

How do you think it'd feel to wholly dismiss the labor of a teenager with your low-effort "ugh vibe coded" comment? I assume you're an adult. I'm embarrassed for you if so.

I welcome anyone to point to any single line in the entire libghostty-vt code base, pull me offline in front of a whiteboard, and ask me to defend it. I'm confident I could. That's how well I understand every line (and on some CPU architecture every instruction in hot paths by LLVM version).

Besides my own understanding, I proudly defend the work of the maintainers of the project. It is high quality and I am thankful for the hundreds and thousands of hours most have donated totally for free to the project (some are paid for a subset of their hours by the non-profit).

To be clear, in the past year, we've accepted AI-assisted changes with a fairly strict policy. I myself do use AI assistance. Nothing goes into libghostty though without real review and understanding. I know that for some, the smallest atom of AI anywhere yields the "vibe coding" dismissal, and you're entitled to that interpretation, but if you're asking me to consider the impact AI usage has, I ask you to consider the real human impact your broad dismissals have.

comments.comment:
I wonder what your thoughts are on the legality of LLM output? I'm thinking of papers like this one, https://arxiv.org/html/2408.02487v3, that find up to 2% of LLM output is "strikingly similar to existing open-source implementations".

It's hugely insulting to me and others who have worked hard to produce [high quality libraries] with trivialized dismissals of years of a humans actual craft and labor.

The reason I ask is because I was struck by how easily that quote also reflects the sentiment held by many open source creators. Trivial dismissal is a perfect way of describing the feeling of those humans that have worked hard to produce high quality software over years of actual craft and labour, only for those efforts to benefit the world without recognition.

You invited the challenge of scrutinising your knowledge of the libghostty-vt codebase. I suspect you aren't aware of the possible 2% of the LLM-generated portion of the codebase that bares a striking resemblance to existing open source implementations. Sure, we all used to copy and paste bits and pieces from here and there in the before times anyway, so maybe that doesn't seem like a big issue. But what if certain non-pattern matchable aspects of libghossty-vt bear a striking resemblance to solutions from, let's say, that very same cohort of non-affluent teenagers you mention? Except this time there is no trace of provenance.

I don't doubt for a second that you would be among the first to provide attribution if there were a practical way to do so. And I don't believe that there is any meaningful way to describe Ghostty as vibecoded. I am just struck by how applicable the overall sentiment of your message is to the very body of weights and biases upon whose shoulders AI-assistance stands.
